Accidentally committing credentials,
API tokens,
private keys,
or sensitive patient data to a Git repository is a security incident that requires prompt remediation.

Simply deleting the file in a subsequent commit does not remove it from Git history,
as the data remains accessible in earlier commit snapshots.

### Immediate steps

1. **Rotate exposed secrets:**
   Immediately revoke and rotate any leaked passwords,
   API keys,
   or tokens.
   Assume that any credential pushed to a remote repository has been compromised.
2. **Purge the file from history:**
   Use tools like [`git-filter-repo`](https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo) (officially recommended by Git and GitHub)
   or [BFG Repo-Cleaner](https://rtyley.github.io/bfg-repo-cleaner/)
   to scrub the sensitive file from all commits,
   branches,
   and tags in your local repository.
3. **Force-push rewritten branches:**
   Coordinate with your team before force-pushing rewritten branches
   with lease (`--force-with-lease --force-if-includes`) to GitHub.
4. **Notify all collaborators:**
   All collaborators must discard old clones or rebase (never merge) their local branches
   onto the rewritten history;
   merging an old branch will re-introduce the sensitive data into the repository.
5. **Contact GitHub Support to clear cached views (optional):**
   Cached commits and pull request views on GitHub may retain sensitive objects
   until they are garbage-collected;
   contact GitHub Support if you need cached views purged immediately.

For detailed step-by-step instructions,
see GitHub's guide on [Removing sensitive data from a repository](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/removing-sensitive-data-from-a-repository).
